#3951. After a 16-year long dev period, Faraway, a shooting star arcade game about siphoning the energy of other stars, is out now

Lord almighty, video games take a while to make, 'ey? Especially if you're just one person working on it by yourself. Such is the case with Faraway, out today, an arcade game that reminds me of the early days of PS3 indies "about a shooting star that creates constellations to stay alive," all made single-handedly by creator of cult-classic mobile game Eliss, Steph Thirion. Did I mention that Faraway took 16 years to make? Like I said, game development is a lengthy process.

Looking at Faraway, and knowing how long it took to produce, it doesn't surprise me to come from a dev who managed to release a mobile game in the early days of the platform, long before free-to-play got its chokehold on the industry. It also really does feel like it should be sitting amongst the likes of PixelJunk, this thing should be something I'm desperate to play on my PS3 while I wait for my controller to charge.

As mentioned, you are a shooting star, a "spark meant to shine and vanish in a blink." But still you persist, connecting to and wrapping yourself around starts to "harvest their energy," in turn lengthening your own life, and of course, in arcadey fashion, racking up a nice score. It looks like game design as poetry, everything you're looking at procedurally generated to bring freshness to every run. I can fully envision this as a "one more run" kind of arcade game, the best kind, especially in an age long past the need to shove in another of your hard earned coins.

Faraway conceptually charms me because it taps into a style of game we don't get to see much of any more. What I'm saying is, I'm just a teensy bit sick of how many roguelikes there are, but that doesn't mean I don't want a game I can just hop in and out of at my own whims. Sure, arcade games might not be in vogue, I just miss them a bit. In any case, Faraway is available to pick up on Steam right now. Seems like it'll be worth a punt!

Last Friday, the very good RPG Nier: Automata underwent what the scientific community calls 'puffer-fishification'. That is to say, it suddenly and inexplicably ballooned to over 700% of its original download size, as an update magically transformed the game from a reedy 50 GB lightweight into a 366-GB behemoth.

But it has since hit the Ozempic and is now back down to its regular size. "We have identified the cause and now resolved this issue," tweeted the official Nier X account earlier today. "Apologies for any inconvenience caused."

Notably absent from the bugfix notice was any explanation as to just what had happened. It might be academic at this point, but I for one would love to know how you accidentally make a game seven times bigger without anything changing.

Squenix is keeping schtum, but Rick Lane suggested, in our article last week about the bug, that it might have been related to Nier: Automata's DLC packages. "When selected for download on Steam, each DLC appears to have the same file size as the base game", he noted. "Weirdly though, this is only true for the initial download and installation. Once the game is installed, the file reportedly reverts to a more appropriate size of roughly 50 gigs." Indeed, the suggested temporary workaround for the issue (before Square Enix fixed it) was to uncheck all the DLCs when you installed the game.

So it sure seems like, somehow, the base files for the entire original game got attached to each individual DLC package. That might also explain why the size increase only applied to the downloads and not its install size—the whole game got downloaded eight times, but it was simply overwriting the base game files over and over.

That's just my speculation though, and without more news from Squenix, that's all we're gonna get. For now, enjoy being able to once again download 2B and 9S' adventures without having to start the download two weeks in advance.

#3949. HUNGER launches in Early Access on December 3

Multiplayer extraction RPG HUNGER will launch in Early Access for PC via Steam on December 3, developer Good Fun Corporation announcd. An open beta test will run from November 27 to 29.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

HUNGER throws you into the chaos of plague-ravaged Napoleonic Europe. This multiplayer extraction RPG blends brutal melee and ranged combat with deep long term character progression, questing and crafting. Scavenge for resources, battle unspeakable horrors, and outlast rival Living.

War has ravaged Europe—but something far worse now grips the continent. A Bacterium of unknown origin has twisted the land, leaving behind only ruin, fear, and something far more sinister. In this multiplayer first person extraction RPG, players will scavenge a decaying world, face unspeakable horrors, and outlast rival survivors in desperate, high-risk expeditions where every step could be your last…

At its core, this is a deep, first-person RPG—one where your story unfolds through the high-stakes loop of a multiplayer extraction shooter. Progress from level one to 100 by completing quests, surviving Expeditions, and mastering a robust skill system that evolves with your choices. The extraction loop isn’t just a gameplay feature—it’s how you grow stronger, build your reputation, and gain access to advanced weapons, rare gear, bags, armor, cosmetics, ingredients, and other vital resources. Every Expedition shapes your path forward.

Players can also choose a unique crafting or gathering profession, allowing them to create valuable items—whether for personal use, to aid their friends, or to sell within the player-driven marketplace. Crafting adds a layer of economic and strategic depth, rewarding specialization and community interdependence.

Whether you venture alone or in duos or trios, survival demands strategy, nerve, and adaptability. The game features no wipe mechanics typical of the extraction shooter genre, ensuring your progress and story persist. Customize your appearance with cosmetics found as loot in-game, trade in a player-driven marketplace, and connect, quest, and transact with others in the social hub known as the Chateau. Proximity VOIP adds an immersive edge to every encounter—friend, foe, or something in between.

As players progress, the endgame expands the core extraction loop with distinct player-versus-player and player-versus-environment experiences—including dungeons, boss encounters, and intense player-versus-player combat—offering ever-evolving challenges for those who survive long enough to face them.

Prepare yourself for a world where death is not the worst fate.

In the unforgiving World After the End, your survival and prosperity are intertwined with the denizens of the Chateau—a broad array of quest givers, shopkeepers, stashkeepers, bounty hunters, and other Living. Completing quests and building your reputation broadens your access to new locations, abilities, characters, weapons, gear, and vital resources.

Deliver fire with a rifle or pistol, or lob explosive glass grenades with an experimental hand mortar. When the ammunition runs dry or the gap is closing too fast to reload, draw your axe or mace to enter lethal hand-to-hand combat. HUNGER is built upon a mix of methodical and frenetic ranged and melee combat as you enter a deadly and brutal dance with both the Hunger and other Living who seek to take what is yours. Find and equip armor, bags, trinkets, medicines, weapons, and shields to ready yourself for the different environments and battles ahead.

While much of your equipment and weaponry may be lost, all experience contributes to progressing your Living and their level. Each of the Living has a set of unlockable unique Passive, Tactical, and Ultimate abilities, alongside deep and extremely customizable mastery trees with more than 100 talents to choose from. Build your Living for stealth and solo play by quieting your footsteps and lockpicking doors. Specialize for ranged combat by quickening your reload speed and increasing your weapon control. Sacrifice your lethality and support your party by repairing their armor and healing them. Survival is the only measure of success.

Explore forests, villages, monasteries, citadels, mines, and more as you and other Living attempt to explore and plunder the remains of the World After the End.

#3948. Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access

I don't know what's going on, and I like it

Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3947. COD: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ patch has nerfed UAV Towers so you're not immediately visible everywhere you go

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 patches continue, with the latest delivering some big changes to the game's extraction mode DMZ. The latest hotfix introduced a key balance change to one of DMZ's most controversial mechanics: UAV Towers.

UAV Towers, previously guaranteed to spawn in every Point of Interest (POI) in the map, have now had their spawn logic randomised. Infinity Ward also reduced their spawn rate by 40 percent, meaning you're less likely to find them across the various regions of the map. As noted in the patch notes, that change also prevents multiple towers from spawning the same area. The only exception is the Deadtown area, which factors into DMZ Order progression and requires multiple towers.

By taking away the guarantee that each POI will have at least one UAV Tower, the patch removes one of the core tactics PvP-inclined and aggressive players have been relying on since DMZ's launch. It's common for players to spawn in, and immediately run around activating as many UAV Towers as possible to reveal the movement of enemy players, even if they're not interested in directly engaging them.

Indeed, some of the UAV Towers cover extraction areas, so it's easy for players intending to ruin the day of others as they're extracting to set up elaborate traps. Making matters worse, a particular character trait prevents UAV Towers from expiring, allowing the scans to stay up for the entire match.

Infinity Ward has not commented directly on that trait, but the developer confirmed it's being changed so the Sedative Inhaler - which hides you from UAVs - also works with those trait-upgraded towers, though that change won't arrive until sometime in Season 1.

Finally, today's update further makes it easier to stay undetected by boosting the Sedative Inhaler's duration to 120 seconds, double that of the previous 60, which should help while we wait for larger changes to be implemented.

DMZ has been one of Modern Warfare 4's most discussed modes online. Recently, players discovered what appears to be a separate matchmaking pool for Story Missions that prevents solo sessions from featuring other players, though with some caveats.

Sony's trail of bodies is only getting longer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sony has dug up another plot in its expanding live-service graveyard, and is lowering the still-warm corpse of Haven Studios' Fairgames into the dirt. The shooter, which was revealed in 2023, has been canceled, though PlayStation says there will be no layoffs as a result of its decision to end the project.

"The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities," a PlayStation representative tells Bloomberg, who first reported the news.

Fairgames was revealed in a 2023 trailer which stylized the title as "Fairgame$." The trailer featured no in-game footage, but presented a stylish version of a Payday-style shooter focused on heists. But the game never materialized again. The last major news on the project came in 2025, when Haven Studios founder Jade Raymond – a veteran Ubisoft producer who'd worked on Assassins' Creed – left the company.

Bloomberg reports that Fairgames was ultimately canceled after a poor showing during a recent test session with thousands of players. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," according to an internal memo.

PlayStation had apparently reworked the game multiple times since it was first revealed, and prior to the test had planned to showcase it again under a new title, according to the report.

While PlayStation once had extensive plans for live-service games, it's canceled so many of those projects that it's now difficult to keep track of them all. The death of Concord just two weeks after launch is perhaps the highest profile example, but that's just the most memorable corpse among an extensive trail of bodies.

A multiplayer God of War title from Bluepoint and a live-service game from Bend Studio were canceled in 2025. A multitude of unannounced projects were iced amid mass layoffs at PlayStation in 2024, including a Twisted Metal game and an original project from the publisher's now-defunct London studio. Naughty Dog's The Last of Us multiplayer game died in 2023. Bungie has reportedly had numerous projects scrapped since it was acquired by Sony. PlayStation has even killed not just one, but two projects helmed by Call of Duty veteran Jason Blundell.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Sony's biggest live-service hit in recent years is certainly Helldivers 2, but it's struggled to replicate that success – heck, it's struggled to release other online games at any scale. The publisher's annual MLB The Show series remains a staple among baseball fans, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls seems to have found a niche among fighting game aficionados, and Marathon is continuing to survive, but these aren't the Fortnite-level hits Sony is clearly gunning for. I guess we'll never know whether Fairgames could've been a hit.

#3945. BioWare are gone, but at least you'll be able to watch their final days in a documentary next year and oh wait that's really sad actually

It feels like every single week for the past few years has been the infinitely quotable 30 Rock quote on repeat. That feeling struck particularly last month when EA decided to shut down the iconic Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. That obviously resulted in the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, of which a leaked trailer and some, now former, devs made sound pretty interesting. But hey! At least there's a documentary coming next year all about the studio that managed to capture the studio's last days! Yeah, I'm not so convinced by this upside either.

As reported by Deadline, Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie will be helming a documentary about the beloved RPG studio for Canada's Super Channel. It's called, punnily enough, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, and will apparently take a look at its origins in 1995 all the way up to its closure and a bit beyond, planned for release in 2027. Filming began two years ago, so clearly this was meant to be much more of a celebratory project than the funeral procession it's going to be.

Some big names from BioWare's history will be appearing in the doc, including its founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip, alongside the likes of longtime devs like Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone. You can also expect appearances from Jennifer Hale, Casey Hudson and, as if his sole goal is to haunt this industry everywhere, Geoff Keighley.

In a statement, co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk said, "When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and deeply moved. BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about the stories brought to life by the amazing people on our dev teams, and the fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Obviously the documentary won't only be about the studio's closure, it sounds like a much bigger effort than that, so hopefully it will be a way to recognise how much of an influence BioWare has had on RPGs. It's just a ridiculous shame that it's something of a posthumous release. Continued solidarity with all those at BioWare.

#3944. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is confirmed, finally getting new trailer and full name, 8 years, 4 months, and 23 days after its reveal

Today, Xbox and Bethesda have finally revealed the name and more information about The Elder Scrolls 6. The game, which we now know carries the subtitle Sentinel, was revealed in a special video that took place today, 3rd November 2026, almost exactly 15 years since the launch of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim and eight years, four months, and 23 days since the first reveal of the title card for The Elder Scrolls 6. That's over 100 months, by the way, or 3067 days, if you want to get specific.

In the trailer, a glimpse of the new game - mostly with some fancy sand physics - before the name, Sentinel, is revealed formally. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate," says a quote in the video, attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell.

"For 40 years, we've explored new worlds, told unforgettable stories, and gone on incredible adventures together," says a blurb for new video. "From everyone at Bethesda Game Studios, thank you for joining us along this journey, for making these worlds your own, and for inspiring us to keep creating. Here's to 40 more."

This reveal comes after a report last week suggested we'd be seeing more of the highly-anticipated fantasy RPG in November, and which also predicted the name of the game. That report suggested that the title will take place in the Tamriel region of Hammerfell, will touch on the "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts". This trailer seems to confirm all that.

Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, as a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside. Notably, the reveal of the game is taking place not six months after Bethesda suffered sweeping job cuts (alongside many other Microsoft-owned studios) as part of Xbox's "reset".

So why has it taken eight years for Bethesda to show us this game? Previously, Skyrim's lead designer Bruce Nesmith noted that the studio and boss Todd Howard felt pressured to reveal the game to the world because "the pitchforks and torches were out". "[...] Todd's opinion - one which I share, by the way - is that the video game industry has short memories," he said in an interview in 2023. "Those companies that start touting their games years ahead of time, actually, you know, they screw themselves. The best time to start talking about it is six months before release." It's worth noting, then, that this is what Bethesda did with Fallout 4.

Does that hint at a timeline for more Sentinel footage being shown soon, and a potentially sooner-than-we-thought release date? Who knows. If we are going to see the game again anytime soon, it's most likely going to be during The Game Awards 2026, which is taking place on 10th December.

I've spent far too much of my life covering the rampant ascent of AI. A juggernaut of tech development, destined to change the world into some sort of sci-fi utopia (if you believe its advocates) or fated to come crashing down around our ears, taking a large chunk of the world economy with it. Or the end of the world as we know it, according to some.

And now, the pillars upon which the AI revolution sits seem to be shaking beneath it. The most recent tremors began with the wobbling of US AI-led tech stocks in mid-October, after a similar descent in China earlier this year. Then at the end of the month, while many tech companies reported huge amounts of revenue in their quarterly financial results, some AI tech share prices still slid under a black cloud of investor doubt.

None more so than Alphabet, the owner of Google. A $500 billion wipe in stock price, led by the admission that the company's own AI search features were eating into its ad revenue, rocked the market. A wider tech sell-off, fuelled by fears regarding the eventual profitability of AI and a potential upcoming Democrat victory in the US midterms, rattled the valuations of many AI tech companies—alongside the chip manufacturers sitting underneath them.

All this, of course, amid a backdrop of increasing AI-related concerns across multiple fields. Rogue AI agents. Increasing AI-powered cybersecurity incidents. Predictions of the end of civilisation, brought on by rampant AI development without proper oversight. Fears of job market ruination. AI psychosis. The list goes on.

Then, the so-called blue wave came to pass. Democrats won control of both the US House and the Senate. Such sweeping political changes can rarely be ascribed to a single factor, but US voter polling indicates that data center expansion was a key source of voter frustration. The current Republican administration has gone all in on AI, and much of the US public seems displeased at the idea of massive AI tech facilities springing up left, right, and center across the country.

Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trillions were wiped off US tech stock values as investors sold off increasing numbers of shares in tech companies, amid further fears that the great AI infrastructure buildout was about to be reigned in by political changes. Long-called-for regulation of AI and AI companies seemed—and indeed, still seems—ever more likely.

And now, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy. At first, it was reported that Alice Huang (no relation) had a "close relationship" with the Nvidia chief.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Now, Jensen Huang has himself admitted that the two were engaged in an affair, and Nvidia has launched an internal investigation into concerns related to national security. The timing could not be worse for the US tech market. At the time of writing, Nvidia's share value has sunk in pre-market trading.

The company is, in many ways, the backbone of the AI revolution, the chief provider of the chips behind the sweeping AI rollout that has changed the tech landscape over the past few years, and the creator of the CUDA platform that underpins it. Huang is its charismatic leader, the relentless optimist behind this AI-led future we're supposedly about to enjoy. A scandal at this stage is likely the last thing any tech investor wants to see.

So, what now? While the long-mooted AI bubble burst has yet to materialise in full, it's certainly looking like the relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end. Investors are shaken, with worries about long-term profitability continuing to eat into the market, alongside US national security concerns now dominating the headlines.

The train with no brakes is rocking wildly against the tracks—and unfortunately, given AI and big tech's role in the global economy, we're all stuck in the carriages behind it.

The relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end.

I'm no economist. I can't tell you if this is the beginning of the AI bubble pop, or whether this is merely an extremely turbulent time in the AI success story. Certainly, it seems like the horse has already bolted, and that AI is here to stay in some form or fashion. Those hoping for a return to the good old, pre-AI days are almost certain to be disappointed.

But, having reported on so many "AI doomsayers" over the past few years, I can tell you that a fall from grace has been predicted by many. Such a massive, world-changing technological development, fuelled by seemingly impossible amounts of investment, has always seemed destined to face some sort of financial reckoning.

That reckoning, I believe, has never looked closer. May you live in interesting times, as the old saying goes. And what happens next? Well, it's going to be interesting, at the very least.

#3941. Take on a time-manipulating corporation in the very Soul Eater meets Jet Set Radio action roguelite CHRONO PUNK

Plus a little bit of Spider-Man, Devil May Cry and Kingdom Hearts

My favourite kind of game that's obviously going for the vibe of a particular era of gaming is one that doesn't look like it's trying to be any other game from said era, moreso if someone told me it was a PS2 or a Dreamcast game everyone forgot about I'd believe you. CHRONO PUNK fits that vibe quite well, an action roguelite that looks like it's taking some cues from those aforementioned consoles, alongside the likes of Soul Eater, Jet Set Radio, Devil May Cry, and Spider-Man.

That is, obviously, a lot of things, but CHRONO PUNK on the surface appears to have its own identity at least. Your player character looks like an almost nightcore version of Sora Kingdom Hearts, with various roles and weapons to choose from; there's a sword and shield, pistols, shurikon, grimoire, and most Soul Eatery of all, a scythe. CHRONO PUNK's got vibes, too. The cities you do combat in are big and nondescript when it comes to details, but ripe for jetting about and Spider-Man-style swinging across the place. And besides, it looks like there's some hub areas ripped straight out of any stylised MMO from the 2000s.

I'm liking the look of the combat too. This'll obviously be one for the combo pilled out there, people who like to bounce back and forth between their enemies like a pinball. Slow paced, this is not. Sick, I hope this is. Pair all of that with some bouncy, wall running movement, and there's some real potential for a strong game here. Sounds like you'll be able to play it in co-op or solo too, which is a nice touch.

The story doesn't seem all that complicated, with some mega corporation manipulating time thereby controlling the city and the masses, leaving you to deal with the mess, but hey, I'm here for the vibes. As of right now, there's no release date attached to CHRONO PUNK, but you can wishlist it on Steam while you wait.

Thankfully, Skyward Sword's director says "no hard feelings"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is, by most standards, a pretty faithful remake to the original game, but Nintendo wasn't scared to make changes where necessary. I was a little bummed to learn the fun references to the Super Mario Bros. series had been removed, not to mention some Zelda: Skyward Sword art that was in the Ocarina of Time 3DS remake, but with how carefully Nintendo positions every game, remaster, and remake into its existing portfolio, I'm not at all surprised.

In case you aren't a Zelda historian, the original game has several Mario references including character portraits and heavy design influences on characters like Talon, Malon, and Ingo, who strongly resemble Mario, Peach, and Luigi, respectively. It makes a lot of sense as Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Super Mario 64 were both being made at the same time, but 30 years later, the remake doesn't share that same connection to Mario 64. That's why the portraits have been removed from the remake, even though it's still pretty clear Talon, Malon, and Ingo have doppelgangers hanging out in the Mario universe.

"Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing," Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma tells Game Informer. "But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, 'Why is Yoshi there?' We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time."

Similarly to the original Ocarina of Time and Mario 64, 3DS Ocarina of Time released around the same time as Zelda: Skyward Sword, which explains the crossover references there. And likewise, they were removed from the new Ocarina of Time remake so as not to distract from everything else going on.

"I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I said, 'Okay, sure,'" says Aonuma, but same as before with the Mario 64 references, "you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way."

Game Informer was kind enough to consider the feelings of Skyward Sword director Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who took part in the same interview, but thankfully it's all water under the bridge.

"It's really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there," he says.

#3938. After taking over EA, Saudi Arabia and their private equity cronies have reportedly held talks about buying Unity

The engine builders have, it's claimed, been working with an investment ​bank to evaluate [their] options

Members of the consortium led by the Saudi Arabian government's Public Investment Fund and some private equity suits which took over EA this year in a leveraged buyout worth $55 billion reportedly have a new target in their sights. Unity, software company and makers of the game engine bearing the same name, have held talks with the consortium over a potential takeover, it's claimed.

According to Reuters, a consortium including Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and private equity firm Silver Lake Partners recently approached Unity about a deal that would value the company at around $25 billion. Unity are, it's claimed, currently working with an investment bank to evaluate their options following the chat, with no deal set in stone right now.

Silver Lake, Reuters note, are already among Unity's largest shareholders and invested up to $400 million in the engine builders in 2017. In fact, Silver Lake's managing director and CEO Egon Durban already has a seat on Unity's board of directors, so will probably have to butt out of any takeover talks.

Assuming the consortium would go the leveraged buyout route, loading Unity up with debt like the EA takeover did, it's hard to see any deal not resulting in similarly catastrophic consequences for those working at Unity. EA laid off a reported 400 people in an effort to cut costs after coming under the boot of the Saudi state and private equity, shutting BioWare and cancelling something Sims-related codenamed Project Lotus. BioWare's demise has since been reported to have largely come down to EA execs not wanting to fund both Star Wars Battlefront 3 and Mass Effect 5, with them opting to back only Battlefront 3.

Unity's recent financial results are looking strong, propped up by year-on-year growth in an AI-powered ad network dubbed Vector, so one would assume that bit of the business likely wouldn't be top of the list if any bloodletting was to end up happening.

Solidarity to any Unity workers who're now having to live under the shadow of this prospective takeover and the upheaval it could lead to if it goes ahead in a fashion which mirrors the EA deal.

#3937. Arc Raiders devs say that using generative AI voice acting was necessary as actors "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

CCO states: "We are not in the industry of replacing actors.".

Developers at Embark Studios, the company behind Arc Raiders, have spoken on the use of generative AI voice acting in the extraction shooter. It's argued that the initial use of generative AI line reads was a benefit to the voice actors, as they: "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that".

This comes from a recently released video by Embark, focused on Arc Raider's sound and music. In it, several key members of staff speak on the game's use of generative AI, be it the initial use of it for voice lines, and the gradual replacement of it with human line reads.

Audio director Bence Pajor first spoke about the struggles he ran into at previous studios; how gameplay decisions couldn't be changed because voice lines were already locked in. He describes this as a "true pain", and that it places stress on the writing team, dialogue team, and voice actors who may have scheduling clashes. He said that using reachable voice actors in Stockholm, and using the tools available, made life easier for everyone.

Later in the video, Pajor explained that training data was made with the voice actor's performances. Due to the voice lines being required for each new feature, item, or weapon added into the game, he argues it would be too impractical to record every possible version of a line read. "The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that," Pajor said.

Pajor continues by pointing to Arc Raider's many updates and changes since its release in October 2025, it would be impractical to call in voice actors to record lines every time an altered line read needed to happen. Two voice actors present in the video - Jo Rideout (Shani) and Diana Gardner (Celeste) - also shared their feelings on it. Gardner said it was "freeing" that she could take a job somewhere else, without worrying about cancelling other shoots or projects.

However, Gardner would later speak on the topic of her ownership of Celeste's many lines in the game: "The contract seemed so fair [...] so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' [...] This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Even with these proposed benefits to using AI-powered performances, these voice lines are being replaced. Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg said: "we are not in the industry of replacing voice actors", and acknowledges that immersion-breaking experiences many players had when playing Arc Raiders and hearing these performances. Strandberg and Pajor both admit to understanding the AI critique, and point to the work being done to replace what they can.

"We are not in the industry of replacing actors," said Strandberg. "Actually I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance and give them more space. That's something I'm hoping to give to players over the coming years."

Part of this critique over generative AI's use in Arc Raiders came from reviews, including our own. Embark Studios faced similar pushback for gen-AI voice acting in The Finals, however Arc Raider's popularity while using the technology led Nexon to describe it as a "trojan horse" for gen AI's use in small team game development.

Today, only legends surround the crystals of Irm. The red crystal of the mountains – once the fire of the great forge, the blue crystal – once the symbol of the knowledge of the eternal academy and the green crystal – once the patron saint of the endless forests; they have all disappeared from the world for too long. Or maybe not after all?

Time and again, noble warriors set out on the trail of the crystals to return them to their original place. Many have failed so far and the whereabouts are still unclear. The legends speak of three dungeons in which the hearts of Irm are said to be hidden. Will it be possible to retrieve the crystals this time?

#3934. "It's a brave new world": GTA 6's PC port will release sooner than you think to avoid losing money to AI rip-offs, says former Rockstar tech director

"If it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."

GTA 6's PC release may come sooner than anticipated, according to former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, because Rockstar and publishers Take-Two will be concerned about losing money to unofficial generative AI clones of the PS5 version, once it launches on 19th November. In general, Vermeij thinks that how to avoid having your games duplicated by chatbot herders is "the big question" right now for devs and publishers, particularly those who don't have the means to enforce their intellectual property dominions as vehemently as Take-Two do for Grand Theft Auto.

Speaking to me during a wide-ranging chatathon, Vermeij reflected on the early days of Grand Theft Auto development at Rockstar North in the 90s, and how the Noel-and-Liam-Gallagher-esque relationship between PC and console gaming has evolved. He shared a sweary anecdote about the company's difficulties getting the original GTA 1 to look the business on Sony's PlayStation.

"I didn't work on GTA 1 and 2, but I worked for the company at the time, and I was actually right next to the GTA 1 team, so I was able to follow it," he said. "So they worked on PC and then an external company in Dundee did the PlayStation version. Which was really weird, because like, PCs were so much more powerful - still the case, but in those days, it was even more so.

"And I remember, at the time, the GTA team was definitely the most rowdy of all of the teams," Vermeij continued. "And there was one particular day where they sent the PC build away, and then it came back from the PlayStation people, and they had cut down all the textures from 256 colours to 16 colours, and my god, the artist was just going around and swearing - 'what the fuck did they do to our textures, I can't believe it, we can't release this shite'. So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console. So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn't really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better."

When it came time to develop GTA 3, Rockstar "flipped that around", Vermeij went on, creating the console versions first. "Clearly the PC market has sort of grown, caught up with the console market, but there's still that same mindset," he said. Most publishers prefer to release all versions at once, Vermeij added, "because then there's only one marketing campaign they have to pay for." GTA lives by its own rules, however. "I guess it's less of an argument for them because the game is just so big, so they just kind of always left it that way. And for developers, it's way easier to just do one version at a time. So, you know, that makes sense."

The arrival of generative AI threatens to throw all this to the winds. Tools such as Reverse Engineer Anything allow for speedy unofficial ports or "slopcomps" of console games on PC, despite warnings from seasoned recomp developers that using genAI for this purpose wrecks the community aspect of unofficial porting, and results in illegible "bruteforce" code rather than preserving some understanding of how the original game was made.

"It really has changed the world," Vermeij observed, "and I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be won't be as good as their effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. So, I wouldn't be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together. Obviously, I don't really know what they're thinking."

GTA 6 is, according to Rockstar and Take-Two at least, an enormously fiddly production, costing hundreds of millions of dollars over eight years in development. Nonetheless, Vermeij thinks current genAI tools are "probably" capable of pulling off a port. "It will take a long time. It actually, physically takes hours and hours and hours to do these things. And it will take a bunch of tokens and everything, so it would probably cost like, tens of thousands of dollars in tokens. But like, you know, if it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."

There are already signs that genAI PC port goldrushers are ready to pounce on GTA 6. Just today, Ars Technica reported on efforts to yassify the game's PS5 trailer footage by piping it through a stronker PC graphics card and using Nvidia's DLSS 5 to apply extra layers of gloss.

Vermeij himself left Rockstar way back in 2009 and is now an indie developer. His current early access project is Plentiful, a hexagonal god sim with an emphasis on water physics. It uses "AI-assisted machine translation for localization", but not for "gameplay content, art, or audio". Vermeij is, in general, interested in generative AI despite the surging tide of slopcomp ports. Smaller indie developers are, of course, more vulnerable to the financial fallout from having their work unofficially cloned by generative AI, but Vermeij thinks it's an existential worry for megacorps like Take-Two as well.

"I don't really see how you could protect against that, to be honest," he told me in closing. "I don't see it. But a big company like Take-Two, they would be able to get the lawyers on the case, and maybe, like, you said, for a big game, maybe the AI doesn't really do a particularly good job. But yeah, I mean, it's a brave new world. What was the case before, is that there's so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that's completely changed now. So, yeah, we're going to have to see in the next couple of years, how that's going to pan out."

The latest rumour-mongering places GTA 6's PC release sometime in early 2027. In other news, Rockstar staff are soon to formally vote on whether to apply for union recognition. If the organisers carry the day, the resulting union could encompass nearly all the company's UK staff below management level.

#3933. Ubisoft and at least two other companies are interested in buying Arkane, according to new report

Arkane Studios, which spent the last several months in limbo following Xbox's decision to divest itself from the studio, has apparently received buyout offers from several bidders.

Arkane was recently given until December to find a buyer and avoid closure, an extension from the previous November deadline, thanks to union efforts. Now, according to a Bloomberg report, a few companies have offered to buy Arkane from Microsoft.

The report names French publisher Ubisoft among at least three companies currently in talks with Microsoft to acquire the French studio. No decision has been made, however. The report also said Xbox considered selling Arkane to its management.

Should any of these offers be accepted, it would mean saving Arkane from closure, potentially saving up to 217 jobs and allowing the team to finish Marvel's Blade, which recent reports suggested is nearing completion. Bloomberg, however, said the game is "expected to be released within the next year or two", so it may not be as close as we think.

Arkane is one of several studios Xbox divested itself from as part of CEO Asha Sharma's big plan to reset the business, which saw over 1,600 job cuts with a further 1,600 to be made by the end of the fiscal year.

Studio divestitures include Psychonauts studio Double Fine, South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games, and State of Decay studio Undead Labs - which have all managed to go independent. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory and Arkane had the biggest question marks hanging over them, with Ninja Theory's fate seemingly the most dire after failing to find a buyer.

Given the December deadline Arkane was granted, we're likely to learn the identity of the studio's new owner in the near future.

EA have stuck a bunch of restored versions and ports of classic games, on Steam, GOG and the EA App. 25 games in all, including multiple entries in the Wing Commander and Ultima series, are part of the haul. Why's this happening now? Well, an EA producer stumbled across a cupboard full of old tapes, film reels and CDs.

According to an interview with The Game Business, the discovery of this old gubbins was a consequence of EA senior producer Jim Vessella needing somewhere new to stick a bunch of Betacam tapes used to help make the Command & Conquer Remastered Collection. "One of the facilities people was like, 'I think there’s a room in the other building that has a couple of items like that'," Vessella recalled. Knowing what I’d discovered with the Command & Conquer tapes, I really felt like we had to find out what was on all these tapes."

The producer was able to convince EA's bosses that this stuff was worth the work needed to stick it back on storefronts, and lo, an EA blog post gushing about their vault's door having slid aside to reveal this pile of retro games. #3930. Guild Wars gets its first major gameplay update in almost 20 years

ArenaNet and co-dev studio 2Weeks have announced Guild Wars Afterlife - the first major update for the game in nearly 20 years.

Coming to PC and mobile, Afterlife will add a new dynamic dungeon that'll morph after each run, and a skill-drafting system that'll allow you to create a distinct skill bar that'll change each time you take it on. There'll also of course be a new narrative to dig into, as players find new characters to interact with, and the new region of Xotecha to explore.

Afterlife is set to release on the 13th January next year, and will retail for $29.99 / €29.99 / £25.99. However, if you pre-order it between now and the 13th January, you can get it at a 20 percent discount.

This is a pretty big deal: the last time Guild Wars 1 got a massive injection of new stuff to dive into was back in August 2007 with the Eye of the North expansion. Following this, ArenaNet would move on to focus on Guild Wars 2 for the most part, leaving Guild Wars 1 servers up and running during that time.

However, the game has itself entered something of an afterlife following almost two decades of inaction. ArenaNet released Guild Wars Reforged - an enhanced upgrade to the original MMO - late last year. It also received a new dungeon in April, which has enticed new and returning players to dive back in.

Afterlife's reveal comes as ArenaNet is juggling development on three live service games at once. You've got Guild Wars Reforged (with Afterlife) of course, the more traditional MMORPG Guild Wars 2, and the highly-anticipated action-oriented Guild Wars 3. All will receive updates and support simultaneously, a sign of confidence in the health of the MMO space.

You've got to hand it to floppy disks. The now 55-year-old storage tech occasionally crops up in the most surprising of places, like a San Francisco light rail line or, previously, US nuclear launch facilities.

One last holdout appears to be the Federal Aviation Administration, which still uses the disks for data storage within the US air traffic control system (via Ars Technica). Not for much longer, it seems, as US transportation secretary Sean P. Duffy has announced the widespread rollout of their long-overdue replacement.

"Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in," says Duffy in an FAA press release. "The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system, and under President Trump, we’re delivering just that."

The ageing disks contain "vital weather and other critical information" used within the current air traffic control system, but that's set to change with the new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS).

"E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” says FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.

"We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System."

E-IDS aims to improve the collection of pilot reports (referred to as PIREPS) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs), with the former representing first-hand reports on weather conditions from pilots to air traffic controllers, and vice versa.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

One of the systems being replaced is called the Information Display System 4 (IDS-4), which appears to rely on floppy drive-equipped machines running MS-DOS. The FAA plans to complete the upgrade to the new system at 435 sites by the end of 2028, with Atlantic City International Airport and Nashville International Airport being some of the first locations to receive the new system.

Here's hoping the upgrade process goes smoothly, not least because I travel through US airspace on the regular. For giggles, I used this calculator to work out how many 3.5-inch, 1.44 MB floppy disks would be needed to contain the 30 GB base client of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

It's 20,834. With fun facts like that up my sleeve, don't you wish you were sitting next to me on your next flight?

3. Best gaming headset: Razer BlackShark V3

4. Best gaming keyboard: Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless

#3927. Airframe Ultra's PS1 cyberpunk city is an amazing tribute to G-Police and WipEout, and I wish you people would slow down to appreciate it

But what if we could gawk at the dumpsters

I do not wish to "rule the streets" of Megacity West, dear creators of Airframe Ultra. I wish to be ravished by them, rubbing my face against the rusty corrugated metal of the shipping containers, and savouring the acid blue waters of the bay. I do not want to "become the one thing with freedom in a city of billions: A racer." I want to become the other thing with freedom in a city of billions: a person who slowly drives or – whisper it - walks around just looking at stuff, because gadzooks, this is one of the prettiest PS1 cyberpunk burgs I've laid eyes on.

Those eroded pastel chevrons. Those seductively wobbling vertices. That electric reef of a downtown backdrop, murderously luring your gaze from the on-coming trucks. That layer of invigorating crackle over everything. Every moment or so, I dismount from my hoverbike to inspect some concrete ruin I could swear I last saw in G-Police, or ponder the resemblance between a subway tunnel and WipEout 2097's Gare d'Europa. Then, somebody waps me in the skull with a stop sign at 300 kilometres an hour. But I was already stopped, frantic stranger! Your brutal poetic ironies are wasted on me.

Despite my best efforts, Airframe Ultra is a battle racer. It's co-developed by Videocult, the people behind Rain World – a game it looks nothing like, but is comparable to in the sense that there is an ocean of industrial refuse to navigate, and you will very often die. Each battle race is broken into sprints around a branching course that has been smashed together by the forces of urban decay. You will corkscrew down storm drains and barge through old abandoned clifftop mansions under a scarlet sun, zip along deadly flyovers and thread the barely legible layouts of high density slums.

Your hoverbike handles like a bronco full of helium, and that's before you start wanging it off the gloriously marbled, low-poly rubbish heaps that stud the city, shunting the game's camera through surfaces and exposing the map's underside in what the absolute squares amongst my readers will doubtless deem "an inelegance", but which true turbojunkeys will appreciate for its makeshift exuberance.

You've got a boost button which generally gets you exploded – and all that's before you get to the time-limited battle arenas that bookend each sprint. Here, players attempt to slaughter each other as much as possible, spending collectible cash on floating weapon pick-ups that range from bent pipes to Gatling guns and EMP grenades. Then it's off for another sprint. The first player to earn 10 points and place first in a subsequent sprint wins the match. I have not won many matches. My primary goal right now in Airframe Ultra is persuading everybody to stop and swap some emotes, while I coo over an amazing piece of graffiti I've found.

My efforts to make Airframe Ultra a walking sim aren't just about scenery. The game is surprisingly engrossing on foot, with some woozy tank controls that make me think of the experimental days before every third-person control scheme became a variation on Assassin's Creed, Uncharted or Gears of War. You have to hammer a button to run, for instance, and you'll wind yourself fast. You can also perform punches and kicks in four directions, with grander attacks to discover by smooshing together inputs. You'd best believe I burst into tears when I realised what this reminded me of: it's Bungie's Oni! The game with the finest martial arts system ever coded! There are more obvious influences, like Road Rash, but in these grim days of endless parrying, I'll take all the Konoko callbacks I can get.

Ahhhhh. But if only this had a proper single player mode. Online and local splitscreen with drop-in bot support are all you get. I wouldn't say Airframe is the most balanced deathracer, either. In my experience, and do bear in mind I mostly try to avoid the racing component, victory typically goes to whoever lands a fat cash reserve and grabs an AK47. That mild shambolicness is arguably part of the charm, in that it supplies incentive to stop and drink in the atmosphere. These streets are big and broken and beautiful enough for all of us, friends. Let us rule them together. Read more on Steam.

#3926. Dragon's Dogma 2 gets a timed collaboration with beloved anime and manga series Delicious in Dungeon, and it's out right now on PC, PlayStation and Xbox

Have you ever seen - or read - the wonderful Dungeon Meshi (known in English as 'Delicious in Dungeon')? It's a phenomenal manga series written and illustrated by Ryoko Kui, which was adapted into an anime series produced by Trigger in 2024. Long story short, it's about a group of adventurers in a fantasy world who lose an encounter with a dragon - who eats one of the party. What follows is a quest to revive the fallen party member (who happens to be the sister of one of the main characters), with the adventuring party learning to cook and eat monsters in dungeons as they uncover the stranger truth behind the world they inhabit.

If you can't tell, I think it's excellent, and the wait for the next season - landing in October 2027 - is practically killing me. It combines two of my biggest loves, cooking and fantasy, in a melting pot of a world that is intricately crafted and a story that is well-told. So imagine my surprise when I saw that Capcom announced a Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen x Delicious in Dungeon collaboration… and that it is live literally right now on PS5, Xbox, and PC platforms, coming in with a new update to the game.

"New allies and equipment are coming to the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with the arrival of Official Pawns and special collaboration outfits inspired by Delicious in Dungeon characters Laios and Marcille," reads a press release from the publisher. "Delicious in Dungeon is a hit manga series created by Ryoko Kui that follows the adventurer Laios and his party as they venture deep into a dungeon, cooking and eating the monsters they encounter along the way. These iconic characters collide with the classic fantasy world of Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen in a limited-time collaboration that arrives today for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC."

For those playing on the newly-released Nintendo Switch 2 version of the game, this update will become available on Wednesday, 11th November.

Official Pawns modeled after the heavily-armored Laios and the elven mage Marcille can be recruited from the Riftstones, but there's a catch: these Pawns will only be available until Thursday, 28th January, 2027 on all platforms. So we've got a few months to play with them, but these helpful characters will not be permanent.

Additionally, players that load their data for Dragon's Dogma 2 during the collaboration period will receive special crossover outfits modeled after the attire of Laios and Marcille. These collaboration outfits will automatically be added to in-game storage and can be equipped by both the Arisen and Pawns. Once redeemed, these outfits will remain available even after the collaboration event ends.

#3924. Terrific fantasy RPG Queen's Domain gets first proper update, adding a new throwing weapon and options to make puzzles "less frustrating"

Extremely good King's Field-style RPG Queen's Domain – or is it a Metroid Prime homage? Or a stealth Morrowind-up? We hacks simply cannot decide – has received its first proper patch, adding a hitherto "missing" throwing weapon, the Grave Knife, alongside a bunch of quality-of-life fixes.

They've stirred in the ability to disable screenshake, alongside some new icons to make status effects more obvious. They've also introduced "options to make some late game puzzles less frustrating", though they don't specify which. How frustrating! Still, it's a tidy overhaul for a game that has rapidly become one of my 2026 favourites.

The big mystery with the update is what the new Grave Knife does. You'll find it inside the Tower of Knowledge, once you've managed to unlock passage. As for those overly aggravating late game puzzles – I find the toughest part of puzzling in Queen's Domain is often just spotting switches and key objects, so perhaps it's something to do with that?

True, there's a large selection of skeleton tableaus who comically point the way to your next objectives, but the game's pixel aesthetics can be rather dense. I very much approve of this on the whole. I like how organic and tumbledown the environment feels - the repeated delight of realising that, yes, you can get over there, and wow, there's a whole other level down here.

Queen's Domain has earned a lot of happy reactions, and is a solid commercial hit. Developers Freshly Baked say it has sold over 100,000 copies, with Vertical Slice reporting that they've already broken even. Glad tidings indeed. Find the full patch notes below, via Steam.

#3923. 2D action platformer isekizima: Ruins and Tails Journey launches January 19, 2027 for PC, later for Switch

2D action platformer isekizima: Ruins and Tails Journey will launch for PC via Steam on January 19, 2027 for $17.99 / ¥2,250, followed by Switch at a later date, developer TamagawaSoft announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via TamagawaSoft:

Explore ancient ruins reclaimed by the forest as Kijino, a nekomata (a two-tailed cat spirit from Japanese folklore). Music composed to match the scenery of each area accompanies the journey.

Set out with Kijino along quiet woodland paths and into caves beneath the island. The journey unfolds across more than 30 stages, accompanied by over 40 folk-inspired tracks composed to suit the scenery. The music gives the island a voice of its own.

As the journey goes on, the island offers new ways forward. Run, jump, and dash past obstacles, swing across gaps on a grappling wire, ride minecarts along tracks that disappear into caves, and take the controls of a golem. The controls are easy to learn, and if you make a mistake, you can retry immediately from the last checkpoint.

Meet new friends along the way, and watch the story unfold through their expressions and in-game illustrations. Seek out hidden treasures and collect outfits to make Kijino’s look your own. New sights and new ways to play keep you wondering what lies beyond the next bend.

Newcomers can progress at a steady pace, while experienced players can try three optional challenge settings, such as making enemy attacks fiercer or capping max HP at its starting value. There are 47 Steam achievements that encourage different ways to play, like reaching the goal without defeating any enemies.

The “Supporter Pack” will be available on Steam on January 19, 2027, the same day as the base game.

The digital artbook features concept art, character designs, rough sketches, guest artwork, story illustrations, and more.

He used to sell gaming GPUs, now he's in the middle of a geopolitical quagmire.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair in a statement published on Nvidia's newsroom. A strange move for the $4.5 trillion company without the added context: the person he's suspected of having an affair with has also been deemed a Chinese intelligence asset by US officials, and was investigated for smuggling none other than Nvidia's own chips.

The story goes far deeper than Huang's affair; revolving around national security, export controls, spying, chip smuggling, and US/China relations. It's in large part about AI, and who controls the hardware that makes it possible. So, if you're wondering why Huang might be the target of Chinese intelligence to begin with, or why he's announcing his affair in the most public way possible, here's how we got to this point.

Nvidia is at the centre of the debate about whether the United States should sell its most technologically advanced chips to China. The US had already ensured China couldn't make the most cutting-edge chips through a ban of Netherlands-based ASML's chipmaking machines. Yet it has also moved between qualified bans of high-performance chips, leading to made-for-China GPUs, such as the RTX 4090D, RTX 5090 D, and H20; to outright bans, namely the ongoing restrictions for the Blackwell architecture; Nvidia's latest and greatest.

There have been a lot of changes to export controls between the US and China, going back to Biden's trade war. Limitations were introduced in 2023 that used "weighted teraflops" and "adjusted peak performance" to decide which systems were deemed too good to be sold in China. It also limited specific cards based on their total processing power and performance density, which nixed specific chips such as the RTX 4090 (and later the RTX 5090).

Both Nvidia and AMD had to build slower versions of their GPUs to try to keep revenue flooding in from China. This itself was a contentious move, with then-Secretary of Commerce, Gina Raimondo, saying "if you redesign a chip around a particular cut line that enables them [China] to do AI, I'm going to control it the very next day." They went back and forth on this approach a lot.

The good news for Nvidia and AMD was that it was President Trump who eased controls on GPUs, such as the H20 and MI308. Both chips were pared-back versions of existing chips, H200 and MI300, respectively, for the Chinese market in order to meet restrictions. The bad news was Trump said he'd do it in return for 15% of their China revenue. That was in August, 2025.

Whether either company sold any chips to China around that time is another matter, their respective CEOs suggest few, if any. Jensen Huang said in October, 2025, Nvidia was "100% out of China… we went from 95% market share to 0%."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

AMD's CEO, Dr. Lisa Su, said in the company's Q3 earnings at the start of November that it had received licenses from the Commerce Department but that it hadn't included any sales in its Q4 guidance as it was still up in the air.

By December, 2025—yes, that's how quickly these things change—Trump eased controls on China again, allowing Chinese companies to make do with last-generation GPUs, such as the H200. To get their hands on them requires a thumbs-up from the US Department of Commerce in return for a 25% fee. One report suggested that Chinese firms were limited to 75,000 GPUs each, which was reportedly half of what shopping giant Alibaba and TikTok owner ByteDance had hoped for. Though Nvidia confirmed later that it had received orders from "many customers in China".

This has proven a contentious move. Not only in the US, where national security concerns are paramount, not helped by reports that the US is approving sales to companies with empty offices and ties to possibly blacklisted entities; but also in China. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) wasn't sure it even wanted the GPUs. It took a while to approve imports of the H200 and that wasn't even the end of it, as there was reportedly another hold-up for imports later on.

The CCP didn't sit back and watch this all unfold without action. It jumped between a policy of lessening reliance on US tech, building its own lithographic DUV and EUV machines, and making more efficient AI models, and blocking sales of specific cards, including blocking the RTX 5090 D v2 in China the day Jensen Huang was visiting. That sends a signal. Chinese authorities even launched an antitrust investigation into Nvidia's acquisition of Mellanox, which was linked to export restrictions and part of the tit-for-tat trade war between the two countries at various points in the past half-decade.

Long story short, and to cut out some of the bits where it wasn't really clear which chips could go where and to whom, there was a long period of time when Chinese firms couldn't officially get their hands on a lot of the most powerful GPUs.

Throughout this entire period of export restrictions and policy changes, there were claims that companies and criminals were bypassing the whole lot of it.

Falsifying customs documents, diverting through third-countries, and purchasing under false pretences are all ways that one might get around the ever-changing export restrictions in both the United States and China.

The US Department of Justice seized more than $50 million worth of Nvidia GPUs from an American business attempting to circumvent export restrictions. Alan Hao Hsu, of Hao Global LLC, pleaded guilty to smuggling at least $160 million worth of Nvidia H100 and H200 GPUs between October '24 and May '25. Hsu and others are said to have used falsified shipping paperwork to try to ship the GPUs to China, Hong Kong and elsewhere in violation of US export controls.

More recently, Malaysian customs shared it had seized $12 million worth of chips found in servers, which were headed for undisclosed countries in Asia. This is a hot topic for the US, which previously noted that it wants Malaysia to keep a close eye on shipments of any and all Nvidia chips in and out of the country, for fears of them ending up in China. A similar case saw two Chinese nationals arrested for exporting tens of millions of dollars worth of chips through Malaysia between October 2022 and July 2025.

A known name in datacentres, Supermicro, has also been mixed up in smuggling claims. The company's co-founder, employee, and a contractor were charged with conspiring to divert servers containing powerful AI chips to China, via a Southeast Asian country, in violation of export controls.

“The indictment unsealed today details alleged efforts to evade US export laws through false documents, staged dummy servers to mislead inspectors, and convoluted transshipment schemes, in order to obfuscate the true destination of restricted AI technology—China,” said John A. Eisenberg, Assistant Attorney General for National Security.

The contractor involved in the case pleaded guilty to the charges in a New York court in October, 2026. The Taiwanese authorities were also heavily involved in the case, working with Supermicro to investigate the company's local offices.

There have been similar cases in Singapore, too, which is one of the largest markets for Nvidia outside of the US, despite not making up a similar share of actual shipments. Companies use the country as a base for operations beyond its borders. The Singapore government said at the time it would enforce export controls and combat smuggling.

Whether these chips end up in China is, of course, the big question. The US has questioned whether major AI models out of China, namely DeepSeek, were trained on Blackwell GPUs despite export controls, suggesting it expects some cards are making it through its ban.

Jensen Huang never named the person that his affair took place with, but he does note the national security concerns arising from it, which alongside previous reports, suggest they are Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. Alice Huang is connected to this saga not only through a personal relationship with Jensen Huang, but how the US authorities came to believe they were a Chinese intelligence asset in the first place.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Alice Huang is linked to Singapore-based datacentre company Megaspeed. US authorities were monitoring her on suspicion of chip smuggling—yep, the thorn in the side of the US' export controls—and the company has faced scrutiny over who funds/owns it and its operations; scrutiny that Nvidia has rallied against in the past.

"We want to be absolutely clear: over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia. These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," a statement on the Megaspeed website reads. It is dated December 23, 2025, and pops up automatically when you visit the page.

Megaspeed rents computing power to other companies and has been connected to Chinese giant Alibaba. There's quite a tangle of connections here, but it's said that Alice Huang used her connections with Alibaba to secure investment, alongside suggestions of securing US chips. Alibaba is also said to have lent money to a Megaspeed subsidiary, Speedmatrix, via its own subsidiary, Apex Enterprise Solutions. Megaspeed's balance sheet grew from $33 million to $3 billion in 2024, reportedly via its subsidiary, the Financial Times reports.

The authorities came to the conclusion that Alice Huang was acting on behalf of the CCP. They also discovered her relationship with Jensen Huang. Though the details of that relationship were not made explicit in the original report by the NYT. Reportedly, Huang had not been briefed on the threat of foreign intelligence, despite his importance and ties to the president of the United States.

Nvidia pushed back on the claims at the time. An Nvidia spokesperson said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."

The Nvidia Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia also holds that accusations of chip smuggling made against Singaporean firm Megaspeed were "thoroughly investigated and debunked last year."

We now know that Jensen's relationship was not as usual or as one might expect of a business partnership. A follow-up report from the NYT suggests that a memo was circulated around the Trump administration last spring (slightly unclear when exactly) that suggested a Chinese spy was close to Nvidia's CEO.

All of which leads to Huang's sudden announcement of his affair on Nvidia's newsroom, and the company's simultaneous investigation into the alleged interference by a foreign intelligence asset.

Prior to his statement, Huang had been asked to attend a closed-door joint meeting with the House Select Committee on China, House Foreign Affairs Committee, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The meeting would be to discuss the concerns of these committees' in regards to Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's security protocols.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen say in the meeting invite. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk.”

The meeting is set for November 18, 2026.

So, it's not all about Huang being so open as to express his affair to the world in the most public way possible. It was probably going to come out at some point anyways, and Huang is getting ahead of it to buttress his own chances of survival and his company's share price.

Nvidia's share price has dropped 16% in the past five days; the drop likely coincides with the joint statements from Huang and the Nvidia board, but partially in line with a wider sell-off in tech stocks. The AI bubble is straining right now.

#3921. Nexus Mods introduces new AI disclosure rules, but won't ban AI mods outright

"We hope what we have planned for now is a good first step."

Nexus Mods, the largest website for finding and downloading PC mods, has revealed new guidelines aimed at properly identifying mods created entirely using gen-AI or those created with AI assistance.

In a new blog post, Nexus clarified its stance on a number of topics, but said it won't ban AI-generated mods altogether. Going forward, mod authors are required to disclose whether or not their mods used AI, and clarify how it was used. A toggle has also been added, giving visitors of the site the ability to filter out any mods that use AI.

Aware of how controversial the decision not to have a blanket AI ban would be, site co-owner Foledinho explained that although "we are pro-human creativity", it would be "difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable".

"An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use," Foledinho explained. "We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform."

That same courtesy extends to mods created entirely using AI, so long as that fact is disclosed. "This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct," the post continues.

The new, mandatory disclosures cover existing mods, too, whose authors have 60 days to review whether their mods meet the new requirements. The new rules come alongside updates to the site's UI, which should make AI tags on mod pages more prominent. Not all backend changes will arrive at once, however.

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that's not going to happen," Foledinho added. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules."

A different (albeit related) problem the deluge of AI-assisted mods introduced is the idea of remixing and modifying other authors' mods, often without their permission.

Nexus Mods doesn't have a solution for that problem at the moment, but the site is "working on introducing new permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods." By the same token, the post clarified the site won't itself use mods to train AI, or sell or license the mods to "anyone doing so".

This could prove to be a more complex problem to solve, given how often one mod relies on another mod to function, and that's saying nothing of contributions from other authors or users themselves.

Then there's the issue of AI-generated and AI-assisted thumbnails, which run the gamut from those entirely created by gen-AI to original shots upscaled or enhanced using AI tools. The post said no new rules governing those cases are being introduced, calling them "grey zones", but that "this discussion is not over yet."

"I'll be honest with you all, there are some details we still need to figure out and work through, especially when it comes to existing licences, forks, and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod," the post goes on. "But we want to get this right, and not rush through changes that could cause more problems further down the line. This does mean that these improvements will take longer to deliver, but we hope what we have planned for now is a good first step, and you'll bear with us whilst we continue to move in the right direction."

Just yesterday, indie game website itch.io was forced to expand its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' threatened to overwhelm the site. Previously, Valve came under pressure due to a perceived lack of curation around AI-developed titles during the most recent Steam Next Fest, prompting public outcry and a demand for more action from the company.
