Silent Hill: Townfall's St. Amelia is a singularly unnerving location, especially if, like me, you are blessed with the good fortune to be a Scot. It's a fictional place, but one that a lot of us are intimately familiar with, even as it's twisted by fog and trauma. It's a nightmare, and like most nightmares it's powerfully relatable.

When I spoke with director Jon McKellan at Gamescom, we talked a lot about Scottishness and authenticity, which St. Amelia has in spades. And with the game now out in the wilds, we've reconvened—this time joined by art director Paul Abbott—to dig deeper into the town's origins, and the process that brought it to life.

Screen Burn knew it wanted to create St. Amelia, and it had a clear vision for the town right at the start. "We knew where we wanted to draw reference from—lots of Scottish coastal towns, island towns, stuff like that," McKellan tells me. "Once you've played through the story, I think the things that have happened to St. Amelia, it's very much because of who they are and where they are. So it was always a fundamental part of the story that it was the type of town it was."

"We realised that leaning into things was going to make things much more authentic."

But what wasn't locked down was St. Amelia's location. "What wasn't clear right away was whether we were actually going to say that it was a Scottish town or just a Northern European town, and kind of leave it very vague." It didn't take long for Screen Burn to settle on making it more specific, however. "We realised that leaning into things was going to make things much more authentic."

The original pitch to Konami described it as a small fishing village with Scottish heritage—something that should feel familiar and nostalgic to Scots, but bizarre to players from outside of the UK. "It should feel like a very new type of environment," McKellan adds.

After 27 years of both publishing and developing Silent Hill games, you might expect Konami to be extremely protective of the horror series, but McKellan says the publisher proved to be pretty hands-off—it was fully onboard with Screen Burn's concept.

"They knew we were passionate about striving for authenticity," he says, "not just in visuals but in the general feel of things—and that having a Scottish team build a Scottish town was the right way to go. Both Konami and Annapurna would regularly play and provide feedback, of course, but I think what was really surprising from the get-go was how aligned we all were on our general ideas and pitch."

It's surprising, given how much of a big deal Silent Hill has once more become for Konami—there's the assumption that big publishers like to meddle a wee bit, or leave developers with challenging restrictions. "It's such a rare joy to work with teams that welcome experimentation and exploration," McKellan adds, "especially on a franchise as big as this."

Konami's faith paid off. When I first stepped into St. Amelia, it was like being hurled back 30 years. The wallpaper, furniture, a thousand little touches, all reminding me of what Scotland looked like when I was wee. "I think pretty much anyone that's kind of grown up in the UK or been here a lot will find something recognisable within St. Amelia somewhere," says McKellan, "whether it's shop signs or your granny's kitchen. You'll find something to hook onto, but then for people who are not from the UK, it's somewhere they've never seen before."

These tiny familiar or alien touches, depending on what part of the world you live in, aren't merely set dressing. The old TVs and crimes against interior decorating ground Townfall with their mundanity, which makes the horror rug pull all the more effective.

"Whether it's Silent Hill-style horror or sci-fi horror, the more grounded and believable something can be, the more it affects you when it goes wrong," says McKellan. "So if you can buy into the world, if it's familiarity or detail or touch points that people can relate to—all of that starts to build a subconscious picture. And when you turn it on its head and flip it, it becomes all the more unsettling. If everything was completely crazy, then nothing's crazy."

It helped that St. Amelia already kind of existed—or versions of it, at least.

"We toured all over Scotland," says McKellan, "and some of North England as well. We went down to North Berwick, down that east coast, and went up to Shetland, which obviously had a lot of parallels, up in Lerwick, especially for the story we told."

Lerwick is the UK's most northern town, more than 100 miles away from the mainland. It's not particularly easy to get to, so Screen Burn only visited it once, but you can see a lot of it in St. Amelia—that cosiness juxtaposed to how isolated it is.

St. Monans, on the Fife coast, was another major influence. You can tell even at just a glance: the coloured houses on the waterfront, the reliance on fishing, the sense, in specific locations, that time has stood still. There are buildings and streets that Screen Burn replicated in St. Amelia almost exactly.

"It's this tiny little pocket town off to the side that a lot of people don't really talk about," says McKellan. "There's not a lot there, but those are the kind of places that captured the history better. Like, hadn't moved on quite so much, so you could kind of see how things used to be a little bit clearer."

It was perfect for Townfall. Pretty, but not lavish; not well known, but familiar. And it's got a bit of bite to it. St. Monans was, after all, named after a Christian missionary murdered during a Danish raid more than a thousand years ago.

You could kind of see how things used to be a little bit clearer.

But the atmosphere of St. Amelia is not entirely unique to Scotland. Abbot is English, and a lot of St. Amelia is drawn from his experiences and local haunts. "I grew up in the north of England, '70s and '80s, and it's quite a bleak place. And there's a lot of that in the game."

As Abbott points out, St. Amelia also captures the British horror films and TV shows of the '70s and '80s as well, "where you've got these empty towns that have just recently been lived in, but there's just this eeriness you recognise, and there's no one about."

Even though there were a lot of references that Screen Burn was able to draw from, St. Amelia feels so cohesive because a lot of these wee towns are already so similar. When the studio narrowed down what it needed St. Amelia to be (not too big, not too touristy), that left it with a shortlist of towns that had a great deal in common.

Its island setting also informed a lot of the artistic and design decisions that Screen Burn had to make, "even down to what stone would be available to build these buildings," says McKellan.

"I think that helped, didn't it?" Abbott adds. "That direction of, well, it's a small island, they've only got a certain amount of materials on that island to work with, and so that just limits your palette, so it ties everything together."

So St. Amelia was locked in very early on, but the path to bringing it to life wasn't straightforward, says McKellan. "A lot of it was evolving with the story, with the gameplay, kind of back and forth."

One thing that stayed the course, however, was that players would be exploring it in a first-person perspective. "From the original pitch it was always first-person," says McKellan. "We knew that searching and exploring the environment, and learning about the town in that way, was a key pillar, and you just don't build the same connection when your camera is five meters away from everything all the time.

"We felt with St. Amelia being 'the star of the show' we should let you really get in about it, and search those cabinets and drawers as you would in real life. It really informed how we built the town, as with no camera to accommodate over the players shoulders, we didn't have to compromise in accuracy or scale. Everything is a 1:1 match with its real-life counterparts. None of our doors are three times the height they should be just to let the camera through."

To create something that so overtly matched reality involved a lot of travel and a lot of snapping.

Because the town is based on real places, Screen Burn didn't need to do much concept art. But it did have to take a lot of photographs all over Scotland. "I'd drive around looking for fog, and take loads of concept photography because we didn't have to paint over it," McKellan says. "It exists. It's there. We can just draw direct reference. So we were driving around Scotland, taking a lot of photographs and building what the kind of visual identity of a town should be, but when it came to the layout, how it fits together, that was a much slower, more experimental process".

One of the first things the team did, McKellan recalls, was figure out all the metrics—"how big should things be, especially in first-person"—which involved using LiDAR to scan entire streets.

"We'd walk around with our iPhones or with our SLRs," he says, "and take thousands of photographs, stitch them together, and build this 3D scanned version in Unreal that we could walk around, and that would give us 1:1 measurements for everything. So we could find out how wide the roads are, how deep the curb is, stuff that most people would never ever think about."

It's a lot simpler to create modern cities—which are often laid out in a grid. That's not how an old fishing village looks. "They all radiate out from the port. So the road patterns are never a grid; they're never simple. Everything's a curve on top of a curve, which is a nightmare to make in videogames. So we had lots of difficult decisions to make in terms of how authentic we'd stick to it, and we decided to go all-in, for better or worse, and make the layout of this town make as much sense as it should in pursuit of authenticity over game design."

McKellan remembers it being a "really long process" to make it feel like a real town while still working as a location for a survival horror game.

But the realism actually worked well with the demands of a survival horror game, he notes. The small streets, buildings squashed up against each other, there's a thin line between quaint and oppressive. "What it means is that we knew that even when you're outside in the fog, you're still going to feel a sense of claustrophobia, and you're still going to feel lost. These towns are really sweet and cute on a summer's day, but when you stick monsters and fog in there, it suddenly becomes a labyrinth, even when you're outdoors in the open."

Despite the town often feeling claustrophobic, players were still given quite a lot of freedom of movement, and that can be a challenge when designing a horror game, where pacing is everything. So Screen Burn needed to identify where to limit that freedom, and how to nudge players in an appropriate direction.

When Simon first arrives in St. Amelia, players aren't able to run, because Screen Burn wanted to slowly unfurl the town and build up its thick atmosphere. And the game is filled with subtle cues and other bits and pieces that subtly guide the player without being too obtrusive. It might be through the use of colour—but no yellow paint—or the composition of a specific scene, or just the lighting. There's gating, too, like locked doors that require a bit of backtracking to open, but after which you're able to create a shortcut.

"Ultimately we try to respect the players' freedom to explore as they want," McKellan says, "and if they want to spend 15 minutes looking at every shop window on the way into town, they can, and it's just up to us to make sure that that doesn't completely fall apart if they do. So yeah, there's only so much you can do in exchange for that player freedom."

There are so many nostalgic flourishes that I couldn't help but slowly snoop around, admiring mundane props that brought St. Amelia to life, like the familiar guide dog charity box, or even just little notices in shop windows. In many cases these are real objects that were scanned or, in the case of notices and the protest placards you find in the town square, initially created by hand.

You've just got to remember what it was like and then recreate it.

Location visits naturally helped with this, and as McKellan told me at Gamescom, the team found scans of old '90s Argos catalogues that helped them create furniture and electronics that fit the era. But naturally there are limits to what can be found online.

"Memory is a big thing," says Abbot, "because you can't just go and search on the internet for '90s packaging design, because there's not a lot of it there. You've just got to remember what it was like and then recreate it. We put a lot of effort into the packaging and also understanding technology and what people were doing with it at the time. So in the family clinic, there's some Word art on the wall. You can't do that in Word now, but we remembered what it looked like, so we just recreated it because people were doing it. It was like, yeah, we can make our words 3D and wobbly now."

The problem with looking for '80s and '90s inspiration online is that so much of the aesthetic of that era has been infected by America and Hollywood. If you were around for the '80s in the UK, you almost certainly would not have been surrounded by neon and vaporwave.

"Especially in the UK, it's just grey," says McKellan. "Grey, wet, dull. Everything's navy. Very concrete. Once you get past the early 2000s, what you find on the internet is very much the stylised version of it, and the reference actually just stops existing. You've got to literally dig out photo albums from your granny's house and start searching through things that way."

All the photos and paintings that you'll find in St. Amelia are real, too. Screen Burn used old family photos to decorate the town's homes, created with analogue cameras, long before the rise of digital photography. Many of the paintings, meanwhile, were created by McKellan's wife's great grandad, Andrew Hall, who died in 1953 but is in the game's credits.

"He was born in the 1800s and was not a famous painter in any way," McKellan says. "He was just someone who did it as a hobby. And then a few years back, we found this collection of paintings that he'd done, and they were just perfect working class Glaswegian hobbyist paintings. And then they become a big part of the game, giving things that authentic feel. Instead of trying to paint a bunch of images that look like paintings from the era, we actually just found them and used them."

As Abbott says, "You just can't fake that stuff." And even before I knew their origin, I spent a lot of time in-game admiring them. Not because they are incredible works of art—though they are undeniably good—but because they all evoke such a strong sense of place and time. "His drawings and his paintings are beautiful because you can just see the way that they've evolved over time, and he does stuff in them where it's like, there's no way I could fake that."

McKellan's wife, Lee, is Screen Burn's art producer, and the team also got their kids involved, giving them paper and pens and telling them to go to town, resulting in all the kids' drawings that you'll encounter. Multiple generations of family members ended up contributing to the game, and together, all these little touches build up to create a place that doesn't simply feel real, it feels human.

Naturally, this creates a disturbing juxtaposition when you are faced with something inhuman—not just the monsters, but corporations as well. The little houses, the post office, the local shop, they all share a space with ugly modern buildings funded by CEG, a corporation that looms over Townfall, and the reason you see all the protest signs at the start of the game. And unlike the monsters, this is all very true to life.

"Having things like CEG funding part of the health center is a very real thing," says McKellan. "When companies move in and take over a town, they will invest in local infrastructure because they have to. It's usually part of the condition of the deal. If you're going to build a giant warehouse in a rural town somewhere, it's going to give most of the people there in that town a job. Then you've probably got to invest in infrastructure and pay back to the community a little bit. All of those things help bring a believability to it and understand the sort of tension between all the different aspects of a small town and how fragile it can be."

Discovering this is also part of the journey, with Townfall's deliberate pace revealing more and more modernity as you move through the game—you start to really see the impact CEG had on St. Amelia, especially in places like Clara Woods, an austere residential area covered in concrete.

"I really wanted to illustrate the difference between a traditional fishing village town that can sustain itself with tourism," says McKellan, "and then what these big companies can and do to communities, and how it changes over time … so it really helps sell the contrast, sort of almost like a before and after, pre-CEG and post-CEG in a way."

But how do proper monsters fit into this very real town with very real problems? Thanks to Silent Hill's penchant for horrors born from trauma, it's actually a pretty natural fit.

"We tried to follow the same rules that Silent Hill's established over the years," says McKellan, "which is that these creatures are visual manifestations of the protagonists' inner demons, or some way connected to them, and they mean something to them, even if it's not explicit."

Screen Burn's take on these monsters is more grounded than usual, too—"more normal looking," as McKellan puts it. "The guy that Zoe sees, the Sorrowful, he looks like a normal guy, and he's in his pants, and he's got burns all over him. It's far less surreal than what people are maybe used to seeing. Though it is still very surreal: the guy opens his chest and needles come out. But on the face of it, at a glance, it's a guy in his pants standing in a hallway, and you're not quite sure what to make of that."

The team wanted to avoid filling St. Amelia with creatures that were immediately repellant—at least in terms of their silhouette. At a distance, they often just look like people. Because they are—they are representations of the residents of St. Amelia who have gone through something horrific, whether it's a great loss or medical mistreatment.

St. Amelia's Widows, which you'll face when you're playing as Richard, are another great example of this. Designed by Abbott, their silhouette suggests a woman wearing a veil—a woman in mourning. But then you get near them and see that the veil is, as Abbot says, "a slimy piece of flesh instead, and then you get the Silent Hill sort of revulsion when you look close". The Widows are also wrapped up in the protest signs that were used to call out CEG after the death of their husbands. They are terrifying and tragic in equal measure.

Townfall's monsters are twisted shadows of victims, and frankly I hated killing them. And that's the point. It's why the game encourages stealth, McKellan explains. "When you're playing as Richard, if you kill everyone or close to everyone, an achievement pops up which is called 'Missing the Point Entirely'. Because you're basically charging around and murdering all of these Widows with a shotgun instead of listening to them, instead of taking note of what they're trying to show you."

And there are layers of symbolism. When you see a burned man, you immediately think that represents someone who maybe dies in a fire, but why is he in his pants? Why are there only burns on one part of his body? "There's a lot of reasons for all that," says McKellan, "and people are slowly starting to pick away at the layers of it, and it's all very much intentional."

The monsters and stealth also informed parts of St. Amelia's design. Once Screen Burn realised that a specific part of the town was going to have some sort of combat or stealth scenario, it returned to the location to add additional touches. "What might be a front door of a building that's closed might turn into one of those storm door hiding spots, for example," McKellan says. "Or we might need to open the space up so that the players get somewhere to hide, and we'd take a building away and replace it with a garden adjacent to another one."

It was important to provide all of these opportunities for stealth in a way that didn't come across as "too obvious or so gamey," McKellan adds, so there was a back and forth between departments as the level design evolved. And that was a challenge. "Some things do become contrived. Like half-height cover, we'd have to think about what kind of objects would be things you could hide behind on a street, and it turns out that there's not a lot of them—there's not a lot of places to hide on an open street."

One of the solutions Screen Burn settled on was adverts stuck to railings—signs for tours and shops and so on. They're not incongruous and if you crouch you can hide behind them. But for all of them, Screen Burn found a precedent first, some kind of reference to base it on, and only then would it go into the game.

When stealth fails and the monsters are coming at you, that's when the guns come out. But that wasn't always the case. Firearms aren't a particularly British thing outside of shotgun-wielding farmers, and in 1997 two consecutive governments, one Conservative and one Labour, created tighter restrictions on firearms, which ultimately led to a ban on most types of handguns. This was prompted by a school shooting the year before, in Dunblane, Scotland. It never happened again. But Townfall occurs just before these events.

"We're right on the edge in terms of 'historical accuracy,' as shotguns and pistols were still around in early 1996, although extremely rare," says McKellan. "For some time we had no firearms in the game and the flare gun was the only ranged weapon, but it felt too limiting to not have any option to 'take a piece off the chess board' from relative safety. It just felt just too punishing. Melee is effective but risky, it brings a different proposition to the player than ranged."

But even with St. Amelia needing to support melee brawls, shooting and stealth, it never starts to look like a combat arena. It's always just a town.

I'm still pretty stunned by how meticulous St. Amelia, and Townfall more broadly, feels while I'm playing. I'm a big scaredy cat, so I don't go out of my way to explore in most horror games (which is probably why I often end up out of ammo and resources, and very dead), but I couldn't help myself here.

The care and attention to detail demands to be seen and admired. But that also heightens the horror—seeing all these awful things happening in a town that could be my own. Not a space station. Not somewhere in the US or Japan, but so close to home I could take a bus there and be back in time to feed the dog.

Horror is best when it's personal. And St. Amelia really makes it feel so personal. For me, but even more so for Screen Burn and McKellan. So what's the scariest part of St. Amelia for the man who orchestrated its creation?

"It's Clara Woods," says McKellan. "Mainly because it definitely hits closest to home for me personally. My first apartment was essentially one of the flats you see on that first road into Clara Woods, with all the dead lying in the streets. While I've not seen that many people lying on the road, it was a very rough part of town to live and a rough time of life—I've genuinely felt like I was being hunted in those places for real, so if some of that horror comes through we've done our job correctly."

#3789. GTA 6 reportedly has 55 Achievements/Trophies, more than both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 had at launch

GTA 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, and ahead of the highly-anticipated launch of Rockstar's latest sandbox adventure, people just can't get enough information about the game. To that end, overnight, we saw our latest leak: the game will have 55 Trophies/Achievements.

In a now-deleted tweet from (in)famous Rockstar dataminer, TexFunz2 - re-posted by the Twitter account iGrandTheftAuto - it appears the game will have 55 individual rewards for completing certain tasks and missions. At the time of writing, we don't know specifically what these challenges are, but it seems none of them will be attached to the online version of the game; the base game launches without GTA Online, and so we can safely assume that all these rewards will be for the single-player only content. GTA Online will drop sometime in 2027, according to Twitch's CEO.

If you've been paying attention to previous Rockstar titles, you'll know that Grand Theft Auto 5 launched with 51 Achievements/Trophies - again, all single-player - and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with 52. So the latest game has more than either game got at launch - and I can tell you from experience, getting Platinum in either title was a very time-consuming experience. Expect the same to be true here, too.

It's worth highlighting that GTA 5 did, eventually, get more Achievements and Trophies: the GTA Online content upped the complete total to 78, adding 27 new challenges to complete. I would expect GTA 6 to do the same… whenever the PC version of GTA comes out, or GTA Online lands in the new game (it's possible both could happen at the same time).

Recently, we heard why a former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect (mostly thanks to AI clones), when we can expect the pre-load of the game (10th November), and how big the final game install is expected to be (210GB). The final game is expected to be so big and dense with detail that no single Rockstar employee has seen the entire game, meaning there are plenty of easter eggs and ridiculous things to discover.

#3788. The Voidjoy Elite Extender only makes sense for Pro Controller purists

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender is aimed at anyone not ready to give up the Nintendo-specific features of their Pro Controller while dodging that pricey new-generation gamepad. Ultimately, its back button feel and placement don't live up to the quality offered by sometimes cheaper, third-party controllers, though its analog triggers make for a compelling prospect as long as you're buying for a split PC / Switch setup with a strong racing theme on the former platform.

Solid, durable connection and build quality

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender answers a commonly asked question with a complicated answer. Is it worth buying a new Nintendo Switch 2 controller solely for its back buttons? If you're still rocking the original Switch Pro Controller, the JSAUX brand's add-on back button attachment stands to save you around $50 on the price of the Switch 2 Pro gamepad. But it's not quite that easy in the grand scheme of the wider market.

The $39.99 accessory slots into the USB-C port on the top of the OG controller, providing two additional back buttons underneath as well as two Hall effect triggers up top (note that these flippers only work on PC). If you're sticking with old faithful for its rumble, NFC, and motion controls, it's a worthwhile endeavor even if it's far from a seamless integration. With the price of Ninty's next-gen hardware seemingly always on the rise, I'll take any shortcuts that manage to evade extra costs.

If you're simply looking to add back button controls to your Switch or Switch 2 gameplay without funding the full $89 Pro 2 Controller price, though, I'd recommend heading in a different direction.

Does the Voidjoy Elite Extender fulfil its primary aim? Absolutely. Is it the best way to bring back buttons to Switch 2? No - and I'd argue it's not even the most cost-efficient either.

With third-party gamepads offering back buttons and additional features like TMR thumbsticks and charging docks, for as little as $29.99 in some cases, the Voidjoy Elite Extender's appeal is going to be limited to those who really can't leave their existing Pro Controller behind.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender is still new to the market and is available via Amazon and the brand's own site. Note that it's not currently on the shelves in the UK or EU.

Nintendo Switch Pro Controller (unconfirmed third party suitability)

The Void Joy Elite Extender doesn't exactly hide itself away on your Pro Controller. The chunky plastic casing curves neatly around the top panel of the controller itself in two panels. A wider base sits flush with the back of the gamepad, while another raised platform houses the P1 and P2 back buttons, swooping up to provide access to additional triggers on the top of the controller. This is also where you'll find USB-C passthrough as well as five tiny little flush buttons for power, Bluetooth connection, on-the-fly button mapping, and platform switching.

Placing the back buttons on this second raised platform quickly became one of the first downsides I noticed as I made my way through the first few hours of Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake. Many of the best PC controllers already using back buttons will place their clackers on the grips themselves. This means a quick action becomes more of a squeeze on the controller's leg than a specific button push. It's also how the Switch 2 Pro Controller places its own back buttons.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

Raising the P1 and P2 clackers above the main base of the grip, however, means I'm having to hold my fingers a good distance from the actual back of the controller to keep them in position. It's not exactly a natural position, and one that worked itself into fatigue fairly quickly. If I ever returned my fingers to their natural resting spot on the back of the grip itself, I would often find myself missing inputs - mistaking the first ledge of the attachment for the buttons themselves during the heat of the moment.

Combine that with the fact that the Elite Extender itself top-loads the weight of the original Pro Controller, leaving my natural grip slanted more forwards than usual, and my time in Hyrule was a little more strained than I expected.

Aesthetically, the Voidjoy Elite Extender matches the black of the Pro Controller well, with a glossy accent around the main base and back buttons themselves and a matte finish on the upper platform. Branding is kept to the rear of the device, with a simple light gray logo printed on the plastic, and functional buttons along the top are clearly designated.

The little flipper trigger add-ons are fully removable, slotting comfortably into the device with two sturdy prongs, and can be reversed for flat storage as well, which is a pretty nifty trick. That physical USB-C connection to the Pro Controller is also rock-solid, with no wiggling or undue pressure on the port itself.

Of course, there are the headlines: those two additional P1 and P2 back buttons - but the Elite Extender has a few more handy tricks in its arsenal. While I was disappointed to find out the analog triggers are reserved for PC use only, they provide a nicely tensioned 1,280-step optical response for racing titles and can be easily stowed away when not in use.

It's not just PC either; the Elite Extender works alongside your Switch Controller on both iOS and Android, with Touch Mapping available for the latter as well. This is done through the KeyLinker App, though, and I have mixed feelings.

The app itself has enough scope to provide a robust selection of controls, even if the interface runs a little on the jankier side. You've got deadzone settings for both the regular Pro Controller sticks and those additional triggers here, with a simple menu of key assignments to play around with.

Unfortunately, even after updating both the app and device firmware to their latest setting, there's no designation for the P1 and P2 buttons in here. Thankfully, setting up keybindings directly on the pad itself is pretty simple with the Fn key - just keep in mind that your settings won't be saved across games like the official Switch 2 Pro Controller.

The KeyLinker software also opens you up to 42-step macros as well as turbo with adjustable speed as well.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender feels like a stopgap, rather than a set of well-crafted back buttons ready and waiting for your original Switch Pro Controller. The clackers themselves are positioned a little too awkwardly, and actuate with a little too high a tension to truly be reliable in faster-paced games and comfortable in more relaxed settings.

After a little re-learning, I was still able to hit the jump and roll/sprint settings I had assigned to P1 and P2 in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but I was often missing inputs after relaxing my grip or by simply forgetting the pressure required to actuate each clacker.

Switching over to PC, my first playthrough of Control: Resonant has been saved by the super-speedy back buttons on the Razer Wolverine V3 Pro. Here, I had to measure my expectations. It's fair enough - a set of $39.99 buttons isn't going to beat one of the best Xbox Series X controllers (with a $199.99 MSRP, no less), and it shouldn't have to to be worth its price of admission. The Voidjoy Elite Extender is no miracle worker, though.

Control: Resonant requires fast spamming of those back buttons in my current control setup for smooth getaways and faster secondary attacks. These tappers are just too awkwardly positioned when set this far away from the palm, and too heavy to actuate for that to be truly workable. These switches were not made for repeat inputs.

While my PC was warm, though, it was time to give those triggers a test in Forza Horizon 6, and I was pleased with how these worked. While the start of each actuation can feel a little stiff, there's a smooth glide downward that makes fine-tuned acceleration and braking all the more immersive. It's a pity these haven't been carried over to the Switch 2, though perhaps the software isn't quite there to take advantage of them, because they're one of my favorite things about this gadget.

It's easy to see the $89 price tag of the Switch 2 Pro Controller and feel priced out of back buttons on the new handheld. If you're moving from the OG Switch to a brand new Switch 2, the Voidjoy Elite Extender represents a compelling budget-friendly alternative to going all out on Nintendo's second-generation gamepad. The placement and feel of its back buttons, as well as the extra front-loaded weight added to your controller, however, would have me recommending a new third-party gamepad instead.

The GameSir Super Nova, for example, is regularly on sale for $29.99 at Best Buy, despite its $49.99 MSRP. Side-by-side, back button handling between the Extender and this whole second controller is night and day, and you're getting a spare gamepad with Hall effect sticks, trigger stops, and a charging dock for $10 less than Voidjoy's price tag.

While it's nearly double the price, the 8BitDo Ultimate 2 will also net you a far better back-button experience with boosted TMR sticks and a range of extra features for $69.99.

There is someone I'd recommend the Voidjoy Elite Extender to, however. Anyone determined to bring the Nintendo-specific features of the original Pro Controller (easy connection, NFC, HD Rumble) to their Switch 2 upgrade, or anyone looking to keep those Ninty features on the original handheld will be interested here. If it's official or bust, the Voidjoy Elite Extender can offer a set of additional inputs that can see you through slower endeavors with a little muscle re-learning at a fraction of the price of a brand-new official kit.

I used the Voidjoy Elite Extender in a Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake marathon, taking me from Link's first moments in Kokiri Village all the way through to the end of the Fire Temple (with plenty of Skulltula hunting in between). I also connected to PC to continue Control: Resonant and test the triggers in Forza Horizon 6. For more information on how we test controllers, check out the full GamesRadar+ Hardware Policy.

We're also rounding up the best Nintendo Switch 2 accessories on the market as well as the best PS5 controllers available now.

Managing Editor of Hardware at GamesRadar+, I originally landed in hardware at our sister site TechRadar before moving over to GamesRadar. In between, I've written for Tom’s Guide, Wireframe, The Indie Game Website and That Video Game Blog, covering everything from the PS5 launch to the Apple Pencil. Now, i'm focused on Nintendo Switch, gaming laptops (and the keyboards, headsets and mice that come with them), PS5, and trying to find the perfect projector.

#3787. The Outer Worlds 2's first story expansion could well be the opening to the series' last hurrah and will have you hunting for a cure to "explosive cell death" in December

Sub Rosa sci-fi drama and a new region to explore await

Since they released The Outer Worlds 2 around this time last year, the world has rather turned upside down for Obsidian. The studio lost a chunk of staff to Microsoft's mass layoffs and have pivoted to making a new Fallout game as a smaller group shoved underneath Bethesda in Xbox's corporate structure.

Given all that, The Outer Worlds 2's two-part story expansion is likely arriving in vastly different circumstances than those the studio might've imagined when they began sketching out DLC plans. Part one of the expansion, dubbed Side Effects Guaranteed, is set to release early next month.

'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd. That said, Obsidian have also made clear that a second DLC in the two-part narrative expansion to the sci-fi RPG is set to follow in spring 2027. So if this does turn out to be the end of the series, with a third Outer Worlds game currently looking very unlikely following the substantial upheaval I mentioned in the intro, at least it won't risk being totally obscured by a Rockstar crime game-shaped eclipse.

As for what this first dose of extra Outer Worlds 2 has in store for December, Obsidian summed it up as follows:

As you pursue the cure and set course for Elysium, an area home to former subjects of base game authoritarian collectivist faction the Protectorate, you'll be faced with the choice of whether to side with Gordon Hazen or Algernon Lankester. Both are agents of black market smuggling organisation Sub Rosa, with one sounding like the goody-two-shoes diplomatic type and the other wanting to "exploit the subjects for his own personal gain". Sounds more Saturday morning cartoon than serious RPG story with serious choices, but that's always tended to be how The Outer Worlds leans.

Rounding out the expansion are new enemies, gear, flaws which give your character build a funky twist, and a bumping up of the level cap from from 30 to 36. Fittingly given I'm writing this on Skyrim's 15th birthday, one of the new flaws is named 'Must Have Been the Wind' after the meme of enemies in the likes of Bethesda and Obsidian's games returning to chill mode after being shot in the face with an arrow or facing some other obvious sign they're under attack. To encourage folks to dive back in, The Outer Worlds 2 is getting options to respec your character's skills and edit how many skill points are dished out per level up via an update alongside Side Effects Guaranteed.

As much as I'm resigned to the series' likely fate as Obsidian return to Fallout and won't pretend The Outer Worlds 2 was great rather than good, I'm still hopeful it can go out with a bang in these two expansions, if indeed this is the studio's last trip to space for the foreseeable future. It's worth noting that if you bought The Outer Worlds 2's premium edition, these expansions are included as part of it and so will come to you an no extra cost.

#3786. Disney Dreamlight Valley The Keepsake Sea release countdown: Exact start time and date

Disney Dreamlight Valley’s big, annual Expansion Pass is almost here, and it’s looking like it could be the biggest one yet. There’s quite a lot to look forward to in this one, so you’ll want to be ready to dive in and start exploring The Keepsake Sea as soon as possible.

Expansion Passes are the biggest form of content drops we get in the valley, so they’re quite an exciting time for the game. If you’re eager to unlock your mermaid form and start exploring underwater, here’s the exact time and date when The Keepsake Sea Expansion Pass will be released for Disney Dreamlight Valley.

The Keepsake Sea Expansion Pass for DDV officially launches on Nov. 18. A precise launch time hasn’t been revealed, but luckily, DDV sticks to a very reliable and consistent schedule. This means that as long as everything stays on track like it usually does, we can expect the DLC to go live at precisely 8am CT.

This is the same time other DLC releases, like Honeyglow Woods and Wishblossom Ranch, went live. It’s also the time the vast majority of updates have been released. The update will be deployed at the same time for everyone, but some platforms, like Nintendo Switch, may take a bit of extra time for it to appear.

If any unexpected delays or changes to the launch time occur, we’ll provide an update here. Otherwise, though, you can check back here leading up to release to see how much longer is left to wait.

#3785. Dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever get a huge XP buff, but power-levellers shouldn't celebrate just yet

World of Warcraft: Forever has received a massive buff to the XP drop-rates of dungeon mobs (enemies), which should make running these instances multiple times feel more rewarding - and may revive an older levelling strategy.

This buff is a 50 percent increase in experience from all mobs killed inside all dungeons. As detailed in this World of Warcraft forum post, community manager Kaivax wrote that this change has been made "so it feels better to go back in for more runs". They don't outright say this is in response to community feedback, but the subject has been a hot topic since the beta.

World of Warcraft: Forever developers have spoken in the past about the decision to deliberately bring down dungeon mob XP to disincentivise power-levelling in dungeons. The idea was that by doing this, people would be encouraged to actually go out into the world and explore it, rather than hopping from instance to instance until they reached max level.

Sadly, a side effect of this change is that doing a dungeon more than once could feel unrewarding. Playing it once is great, as you get to complete lots of quests that reward guaranteed items and XP. However, if you go back again, you don't get these, so your only source of progression comes from a heavily decreased XP rate.

Some quests exacerbate this issue. Dungeons like Wailing Caverns and especially Blackfathom Deeps have a quest that can't really be completed in one run due to a reliance on drop rates for items you need, and having to fight for drops with the rest of your dungeon party. Having to go back to complete this used to suck, and now it sucks less!

So does this mean farming dungeons to power-level is back? Maybe, but it still won't be nearly as efficient as it was in older versions of Classic WoW. The current mob XP rates, after this buff, will still only be 36 percent of the original Classic rate - a third. Given how fast you can level by doing quests out in the world, it seems dungeon farming isn't due for a comeback just yet.

After an especially smooth launch, World of Warcraft: Forever has become the biggest launch in the series' history, beating out Wrath of the Lich King, Cataclysm, and all the other past expansion launches. The developers have been quick to hotfix things on the fly, including a change that left PvP battlegrounds heavily advantaged for the Horde.

Developer of entertainment products and pillar of the global economy Rockstar has announced that Grand Theft Auto 6, its much-ballyhooed upcoming Bonnie and Clyde simulator, will be targeting 30 frames per second on consoles. Coincidentally, "on consoles" is the only place Rockstar has currently announced the game is releasing, so GTA 6 is a 30-fps-or-bust experience for the foreseeable future.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life", say the boys and girls in Edinburgh, while offering a little sweet treat to PlayStation 5 Pro owners in the form of PSSR (PlayStation of Soviet Socialist Republics—no, wait, sorry, PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) support and ray-traced shadows.

Why am I telling you this on PC Gamer dot com? Partially because the traffic gods would beat me with a roll of pennies in a sock if I passed up an opportunity to write about GTA 6, but mostly because I'm very smug, and wish to subject other people to that.

Let's be real, the odds that GTA 6 was gonna target 60 fps on the box you have under your TV were always slim to none, but hearing it makes me feel more vindicated in my choice to wait for the game to hit PC than ever. I'm sure Rockstar's tech magi will make it a very nice 30 fps indeed, but my TV has 120 hertz in it. My monitor? 144, which I gather is kind of on the low end these days.

When it comes time for me to luxuriate in the lights of Leonida, I want to do it with maximum butteriness, I want all the bells and whistles set to 'on', and I want to do it on a proper gaming platform (German Linux). I'm excited to hear people's reports about what this game's actually like when it finally hits consoles in just over a week, but personally? I've never been happier about my choice to wait for GTA 6's inevitable but unannounced PC port.

#3783. Lootboxes, pay-to-win, virtual currencies and other blights unto gaming face heavy regulation as the EU tables new Digital Fairness Act

It's been 10 years since I lasted opened a lootbox, I think. Just thought you should know.

Loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today. The full draft text of the regulation leaked earlier in the week. If it passes into law - and there's plenty of debate and revision ahead - it'll have big consequences for the developers and publishers of games like Overwatch, Dota 2, and GTA Online.

You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site. The organisers have also published an introductory explainer that takes us through the timeline of the Act's gestation, dating back to 2020, and summarises its provisions. If passed, the Act will apply to any company doing business in the EU, not just those based in member states, with individual governments able to impose fines and consumers able to seek financial compensation if they think they've been harmed.

Here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text. The Act proposes a number of provisions regarding "unfair" commercial practices, including omission and distortion in advertising and PR communication at large. Amongst other things, it takes aim at "dark patterns" – that is, "visual, auditory and other components" of online interfaces that are designed to manipulate or deceive. The text also forbids personalised advertising and pricing aimed at children, and prohibits influencers from making "direct exhortations to minors to buy products or to persuade their parents or other adults to buy products in commercial communications".

The items that are probably of greatest interest to us smelly gamers are the passages on virtual currencies, "variable reward systems", and addictive design.

The Act would require game publishers who sell virtual currencies to indicate the real-world monetary value of the currency and anything bought with it. It would also require companies to disable paid-for virtual currencies by default for kids, unless a parent or guardian has given approval.

As for paid-for "variable reward systems", aka "loot boxes", "surprise mechanics", "Schrödinger's Giftbombs" or however publishers may prefer to describe them, the Act would require companies to state the "types" of object they might cough up, together with the probability of obtaining them. It would also oblige publishers to disable paid-for "variable reward systems" for minors, and give everybody an "easily accessible" way to switch them off.

The draft Act outright prohibits "pay-to-progress and pay-to-win mechanisms" for kids. More generally, it suggests further constraints for publishers and developers who "design, organise or operate their digital products in a manner that is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen to encourage compulsive or excessive use". Again, it wants companies to give people options to switch these features off.

That includes "features enabling automatic play of content and uninterrupted content consumption without effective and regular interruption moments that enable deliberation by the consumer on their willingness to consume more content". Also, "notifications not triggered by, or not directly related to, the consumer’s interaction or activity on the service", "features incentivising engagement at regular times or with greater frequency, including through penalties or loss of benefits", and "features and system behaviours that encourage continued use by simulating interpersonal relations," such as nagging prompts.

If you'd like a more 'expert' account of the Digital Fairness Act - how dare you! I have read several Wikipedia pages about all this - the bespectacled nabobs of GamesIndustry.biz went and got notes from an actual lawyer. All this follows a change in EU rating law last month aimed at safeguarding the weans from predatory habit-forming devices and instruments of financialisation - games with lootboxes are now PEGI 16 by default, while blockchain games are always rated 18. Across the pond, meanwhile, lawsuits are underway in New York and Washington against Valve's tolerance of lootboxes on Steam, which the lawyers in question define as illegal gambling.

Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks have been filtering onto the shelves in the last week, following the Ocarina of Time remake's release date on November 5. With a number of stores bringing 40th Anniversary edition consoles to the party during midnight releases, or well-timed online drops, many lucky stock hunters managed to snag their handheld in time to face Ganondorf.

Right now, there's no Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock live on the shelves, and even finding that Pro Controller or carry case is proving difficult. There's a ray of hope to be had here, though.

In the last week, Target and Nintendo have both dropped new Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks, while Walmart's had the special edition gamepad on the shelves. GameStop is prioritizing in-store orders only, so your best bet is to head down to your local store to check on their inventory.

In the UK, Amazon has been rolling out its restocks in smaller waves, running through last week, over the weekend, and once again on Monday.

Here's hoping we'll see more Legend of Zelda Switch restock action in the coming days - we'll be covering all of it live right here.

I've been tracking hard-to-find stock for over six years now, starting with the incredibly limited releases of the PS5 and Xbox Series X. I've been reporting on how retailers operate with high-demand products, from anniversary releases to brand new consoles, ever since then - including the Nintendo Switch 2 itself.

Amazon has been quieter for restocks since it dropped its first round of handhelds at launch. Still, there's been a good amount of time since release day - enough for the online retailer to potentially re-fill its warehouses?

Walmart's had a bit of a time of it. The retailer cancelled a number of pre-orders just the day before launch, and has been catching up on its backlog ever since. While new stock might be already allocated to those burned by pre-order mishandling, it's worth keeping an eye on any movement here.

Target has been the most active of US retailers in the last week, running scheduled in-store and online restocks around November 5-6 last week. While that inventory might take some time to re-emerge, it's worth keeping an eye for accessories here as well.

Best Buy kept its most recent allocation of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock for its midnight Ocarina of Time launch event. Since then, the online side of this retailer has been pretty quiet.

Nintendo itself has held its own online Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks pretty regularly since launch. This is always one to keep an eye on.

GameStop is only running Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks in stores, so you won't find any online stock here. That goes not just for the console, but for the Pro Controller and carry case as well.

Amazon UK has been dropping Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks in smaller waves over the last week, so it's always worth keeping that tab open and regularly checking back.

EE has offered Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks twice since launch, and has also been offering additional discounts on Ocarina of Time and Pokemon Pokopia bundles as well.

Smyths Toys was one of the first retailers to drop its original wave of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock when the handheld was announced, so we're expecting more action here in the near future. It's also one of the only UK retailers I'm seeing with listing pages up for the Pro Controller and carry case.

Here's the thing with Very. It often bundles up difficult-to-find stock with extra accessories or games to keep resellers at bay. That means you'll be paying a little more here (though still only RRP for everything you're getting) but stock often holds out a lot longer.

Argos was previously offering Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock ahead of launch, but things look to have run dry now. The store organises its inventory by postcode, though, so it's always worth checking your local area's delivery and collection options.

Currys previously had a listing page up for the Legend of Zelda Switch 2, but it seems to have disappeared now, instead sending us to a generic consoles search page.

Nintendo has also stated more stock is on the way, so you'd expect its own store to be one of the first with fresh handhelds up for grabs.

Here we go again, another week of tracking all the latest Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks

#3781. London department store Selfridges launches sizeable GTA 6 takeover, featuring a varsity jacket that costs an eye-watering £2,500

Expensive British department store Selfridges has launched a sizeable Grand Theft Auto 6 takeover, completely making-over its Oxford Street London Corner Shop store and offering a considerable line of clothing, which includes an exclusive varsity jacket that costs a bank-melting £2,500. Note, you can buy the GTA 6 items online as well.

Live from Selfridges at Oxford Street for the #GTAVI activation🌴Rockstar are not messing around 🤯 pic.twitter.com/vqqXKwB1oJ

That GTA 6 varsity jacket is by far and away the most expensive item (and it's apparently already sold out), next to a non-exclusive varsity jacket that's £1,750, whereas the other items are pricey but conceivably affordable.

There are a few ranges on offer. There's a nice bright teal and pink-coloured range based around the spoof NFL team the Vice City Manatees, which includes a manatee plushie, an American football, a jacket, and other bits and bobs. There's also a range based around the spoof NBA team, the Vice City Narcos, that includes a basketball (there's a standard GTA 6-branded basketball too).

There's a range based on the spoof fast-food chain Burger Shot, which includes a visor, work uniform, and apron, amusingly. There are some admirably horrid postcard-decorated shirts and shorts, and there's a lot of generic game-branded caps and T-shirts besides, all in quite nice colours. Quirky branded offerings include an ashtray, money clip and dartboard. It's all quite attractive stuff.

There's no word on how long the items will be stocked for or that the Selfridges Corner Shop takeover will run for, other than "while stocks last".

#3779. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

Those birds kept stealing all my good cards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's worse than fighting one human-sized bird with sunglasses? Fighting two human-sized birds with sunglasses. That wasn't a usual problem in my everyday life until I started playing Stack Order's demo, the hand-drawn deckbuilder that's full of duels and fantastic combos.

The run began with my masked character locked away in a jail cell, not all that dissimilar to how I start most of my days. However, this time I was promptly freed by a stranger who wanted to help out. After handing me a deck of cards and talking me through how to use it, I was left to go on my merry way. The only problem was that I didn't get very far before a knight called Robert, who was very unhappy to see me out of my cell, butted in.

I've played my fair share of deckbuilders so it wasn't exactly a steep learning curve. But unlike some other games, Stack Order puts a very strong emphasis on stacking cards. You need to lose the bad habit of just playing one card at a time and instead start stacking cards at the first chance you get.

But, crucially, stacking cards doesn't necessarily mean you have to use them, you could get everything ready and then forfeit your go or just use a throwaway attack. Most killing blows in Stack Order come down all at once after you've stacked several cards all with varying multipliers and unleash it all at once.

Certain cards, for example, deal extra damage if they come before or after cards, others add damage to specific cards if they're stacked below them. You get a random assortment of cards on each turn, so you can't always bet on a dream stack, but if you're smart you can usually create one hell of a combo.

The only problem is that you're not the only one who can pack a punch. Each enemy I came up against had their own set of skills which changed the fight. Knight Robert had a simple yet effective attack / block combo, the Queen slowly poisoned me, but the birds, those two damn birds really topped it all.

First off there were two of them, which meant extra attacks, but to make matters worse each bird had a special effect that would see them deal extra damage the more cards you left on the table and would steal either the top of bottom card of each stack and use it to buff themselves, including how much they were able to heal. This made things really tricky.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I quickly found out that if I didn't kill them quickly we'd roll into a painfully long stalemate, as I would just barely hang on with shields and they were able to heal 11 damage every third turn. Damage them enough and you can break some of their attacks, they'll still deal damage but won't get the bonus perk.

Managing how you build stacks, when you can't build multiple and also need to leave a sacrifice card for one of the birds to eat, is taxing to be sure. But that's what makes winning fights in Stack Order all the more rewarding.

I managed to experience this euphoria after I bested the pair of birds, but that wasn't the last I'd see of them as, after dying to the next boss, I had to restart my run. Soon I was fighting Robert, the Queen, and the dastardly bird duo all over again, and let me tell you it does not get easier the second time you fight them.
